newsitem.title: USA: J.C. Penney writes Rx to cure department stores.
newsitem.headline: J.C. Penney writes Rx to cure department stores.

text.p: J.C. Penney Co. Inc., a hungry pursuer of drugs stores during the last year, believes it has a prescription to cure its ailing department stores.
Penney opened the throttle on expansion two years ago and, by February, had cemented the No. 4 position in the U.S. drug store industry by buying Eckerd Corp. for $3.3 billion.

But while Penney was bulking up on drug stores, its 95-year-old department store division faltered. Sales have been weak and the stores have been swimming in excess merchandise. Earnings per share for the second quarter, which are scheduled to be reported next week, are expected to be flat.

"At our Penney stores, we've managed to bring balance back to our inventory position while trying to control any negative impact that might have (on profits) during the first and second quarters this year," Donald McKay, chief financial officer, said in an interview Friday. "We basically have the inventory issue behind us."

In addition to shrinking inventories, the company is stocking sharper apparel lines, opening more J.C. Penney home stores -- a total of 35 will be launched by the end of next year -- and running an estimated $20 million ad campaign with the tagline "J.C. Penney - I Love Your Style" to help lift results at its core division, McKay said.
"Our team is feeling pretty good about the fashion offerings," he said. "We expect good profit results for the second half."
Some Wall Street analysts, however, say Penney's management took its eye off the ball while chasing down acquisitions, and the company still has not come up with a formula for fixing its stores.
"Seventy percent of their business is not performing," said Linda Kristiansen of Schroder & Co. Inc. "That's what I'm focused on."

Wall Street analysts estimate Penney's earnings per share will be flat in the second quarter, due partly to additional shares issued in the Eckerd deal. In the second quarter of last year, Penney earned $93 million, or 37 cents a share.
When the Eckerd deal was unveiled by Penney last year, it was touted as a major growth opportunity for the company that would blend well with its department store business.

The aggressive expansion of Penney's pharmacy business marked a decidedly more aggressive approach by a company that had seemed content devoting excess cash to share repurchases, dividend hikes and small department store acquisitions.

With its presence in shopping malls already near saturation, W.R. Howell, who retired as chairman in January, and Chief Executive James Oesterreicher recognised that Penney needed a new engine to drive growth, analysts said. So last year the company went on an unprecedented shopping spree.

In February of that year it made an unsuccessful bid for Dayton Hudson Corp. Undaunted, it turned to drug stores and bought Fay's Inc., a chain of 272 pharmacies, for $353 million last October. Penney combined Fay's with its 645-store Thrift drug division, which was renamed Eckerd this year.
Penney denied its management was distracted during the company's pursuit of acquisitions.
"We decided it would be a unique opportunity to become a leader in an industry we were already in," McKay said. "That was just an extension of what we had already begun."
Still, Penney decided to spread its wings at a time other retailers, such as Sears, Roebuck and Co., have turned their focus to their core retail businesses.

Eckerd is expected to add to Penney's earnings beginning next year. The company plans to open about 150 new drug stores a year while its department store count of about 1,225 is expected to remain steady.

While the goods Eckerd sells are not as profitable as department stores merchandise, Eckerd is a less expensive business to run. In addition, it has huge market share in states such as Florida and Texas, where large populations of retired customers boost its profitable prescription business.

"If the core Penney business stabilises and Eckerd achieves the growth that's expected, people will probably have a more favourable view of the transaction in 1998 than they did in 1997," said Wayne Hood, analyst at Prudential Securities.
Penney's stock was up 87.5 cents to $58.50 in midday trading on the New York Stock Exchange.
